name: Synthetic Portraiture
title: Synthetic Portraiture
answer: Synthetic portraiture is the creation of lifelike images of human faces and figures using generative image models rather than a camera. It covers fictional people who have never existed, reimagined versions of real individuals with permission, and hybrid images that combine photographed elements with generated skin, hair, and lighting. The field sits between portrait photography, CGI, and painting, and it is used in advertising, film previsualization, game character design, and personal avatars. This site tracks 1,000 live image generation models, many of which can produce synthetic portraits at photographic resolution. The key distinction from traditional retouching is that the core likeness is generated from noise or latent representations, not captured by a lens.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Synthetic portraiture runs on large diffusion models and generative adversarial networks trained on datasets of real human photographs. These models are typically accessed through cloud APIs or run locally on consumer GPUs, with fine-tuned checkpoints and low-rank adaptations used to steer a model toward a particular face, age, or style. The site's count of 1,000 live image generation models reflects the range of available backends, from open source releases to closed commercial services. Inference requires enough memory to hold the model weights and a denoising scheduler, and batch generation for casting or character design often uses multiple GPUs or cloud instances. Face restoration and upscaling models are commonly chained after the base generator to sharpen eyes, skin texture, and hair.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a text prompt describing the person, pose, lighting, lens, and mood, often combined with a reference image for identity or composition. Artists then iterate by adjusting the prompt, changing the random seed, and using negative prompts to suppress artifacts like extra fingers or plastic skin. Inpainting is used to fix specific regions such as eyes, teeth, or hands, while outpainting extends the frame or changes the background. ControlNet and similar conditioning tools let the creator lock a pose, depth map, or facial landmarks so the generated portrait matches a planned layout. The final image usually passes through upscaling, color grading, and sometimes a light pass in a photo editor to match the grain and tone of a real photograph.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Synthetic portraiture raises direct questions about consent, likeness rights, and the risk of deepfake misuse. A model may reproduce features of real people from its training data, and using a living person's face without permission can trigger right of publicity or privacy claims in many jurisdictions. Provenance standards such as C2PA and visible or invisible watermarking are becoming common for published synthetic portraits, but they are not yet universal. The site's tracking of 92 active intellectual property lawsuits shows how unsettled the legal treatment of generated images remains. Common practice is to document prompts, seeds, and model versions, and to treat any portrait of a real, identifiable person as requiring explicit consent before commercial use.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Synthetic portraiture is moving toward real-time generation, where a model can produce a coherent face from a few words or a rough sketch in under a second. Video portraits and talking-head avatars are becoming more stable, with lip sync and expression transfer handled by separate models. The next few years will likely bring tighter control over identity, so a brand or studio can keep a consistent fictional character across hundreds of images and videos. Detection and authentication tools are improving in parallel, and many platforms now label AI-generated portraits automatically. As the 1,000 live image generation models tracked by this site continue to evolve, the boundary between a photograph and a synthetic portrait will depend more on provenance records than on visual inspection.
